What the record shows•Congress declares war, but presidents direct limited military force.Article I grants Congress the power to declare war. Article II designates the President as Commander in Chief. U.S. law and long-standing practice distinguish between declared war and limited military actions, enforcement operations, and targeted strikes.•Presidents of both parties have used force without prior authorization.Military actions in Kosovo, Libya, Syria, Yemen, and global counterterror operations occurred without formal declarations of war. In most cases, Congress objected politically but did not block the operations.•The War Powers Resolution has limited enforcement mechanisms.The Resolution requires notification and sets time limits, but it relies on Congress to assert itself. Courts rarely intervene, leaving funding and legislation as Congress’ primary tools.•Targeting or capturing foreign leaders is not inherently unconstitutional.The U.S. has previously captured or removed foreign leaders without declared wars, including Manuel Noriega and Saddam Hussein. Legality depends on scope, authorization, and justification, not simply the individual’s title.•“No regime change” statements often coexist with coercive actions.Administrations of both parties have denied pursuing regime change while taking actions that weaken or remove leadership. This ambiguity is a recurring feature of U.S. foreign policy, not a new development.•Congress retains authority but must choose to exercise it.If war-powers resolutions fail, that reflects congressional decision-making. Congress still holds the power to restrict funding, demand oversight, or legislate limits on executive action.
